nodes.title: Serverless functions: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Functions-as-a-Service (Lambda, Azure Functions, Cloud Functions) execute short-lived code in response to events. No servers, no patching, auto-scaling. The exam tests triggers, integration patterns, and the limits that bite at scale.

flashcards.back: HTTP request (API Gateway, HTTP trigger), object storage event (file uploaded), queue message (SQS, Service Bus, Pub/Sub), schedule (cron / EventBridge), database stream (DynamoDB Streams, Change Feed). One function, many possible triggers — the runtime hands you the event payload.

flashcards.front: What is the function's execution context?
flashcards.back: The runtime environment that persists between invocations on the same warm instance. Things defined OUTSIDE the handler (DB connections, cached secrets, imported modules) are reused on the next invocation — huge perf win. Anything inside the handler runs every time.

flashcards.front: Idempotency — why does serverless need it?
flashcards.back: Most event sources retry on failure: SQS delivers at-least-once, S3 events can fire twice for a single upload, EventBridge retries on 5xx. Your function MUST tolerate the same event twice (use idempotency keys, conditional writes, dedup tables) or you'll double-charge a customer.

AWS Lambda's account-level concurrency cap is 1000 by default. A sudden traffic spike can starve other functions in the account. Mitigations: reserved concurrency (guarantees a slice for a critical function), provisioned concurrency (pre-warmed instances), per-function quotas.

questions.q: A developer is building an ASP.NET Core web app that must run on Linux containers in Azure with automatic HTTPS, deployment slots and integrated authentication. Which compute service should they choose?
choices: Azure Service Fabric Mesh stateless service cluster
Azure Container Instances fronted by Application Gateway
Azure App Service for Linux with deployment slots and Easy Auth
Azure Batch with a low-priority node pool and autoscale
questions.explanation: Azure App Service for Linux is a fully managed PaaS that natively supports Linux containers, custom domains with free TLS certificates, deployment slots for staging/production swaps, and built-in authentication via Easy Auth. Service Fabric Mesh has been retired and never offered managed Easy Auth or slot swaps. Azure Container Instances are single-tenant container hosts with no deployment slots and no managed identity for App Service Authentication. Batch is purpose-built for parallel HPC, rendering and finite job workloads, not long-running web servers — autoscale alone does not turn it into a web platform.

questions.q: An application stores millions of small JSON documents that must be queried by partition key with single-digit-millisecond latency at global scale. Which Azure service is BEST suited?
choices: Azure Table Storage with geo-redundant replication
Azure Cache for Redis with AOF persistence enabled
Azure Cosmos DB account on the NoSQL (Core) API
Azure SQL Database with read replicas in two regions
questions.explanation: Azure Cosmos DB is a globally distributed multi-model database that guarantees single-digit-millisecond reads and writes and 99.999% availability across regions. The NoSQL (Core) API is the JSON document model queried efficiently by partition key. Table Storage is cheaper but its latency SLA is bounded at 10 ms and it has no multi-region writes. Azure SQL is relational — read replicas help reads but not key-lookup latency at global scale. Redis is a volatile cache, not durable primary storage even with persistence enabled.

questions.q: An Azure Cosmos DB account replicates across three regions and is configured for multi-region writes. The team wants the highest consistency level that remains compatible with that topology. Which level should they choose?
choices: Strong, providing linearisable reads against a single write region
Bounded staleness, capping read lag at K versions or T seconds
Session, guaranteeing ordering only within one client session scope
Consistent prefix, ordering without a bounded staleness window
questions.explanation: Bounded staleness is the strongest Cosmos DB consistency level compatible with multi-region writes; reads lag writes by at most K versions or T time. Strong consistency requires a single write region, so it cannot coexist with multi-region writes. Session only guarantees read-your-writes within a single client session — weaker than bounded staleness. Consistent prefix guarantees that reads never see out-of-order writes but offers no staleness window — weaker than bounded staleness.

questions.q: A developer wants an Azure Function to run on the first day of every month at 03:00 UTC. Which trigger and configuration should they use?
choices: Timer trigger with NCRONTAB expression "0 0 3 1 * *"
Timer trigger with NCRONTAB expression "0 3 0 1 * *"
Logic App recurrence calling an HTTP-triggered Function
Event Grid trigger filtered on a month-start system event
questions.explanation: Azure Functions Timer triggers use a 6-field NCRONTAB syntax: {second} {minute} {hour} {day} {month} {day-of-week}. "0 0 3 1 * *" means second=0, minute=0, hour=3, day=1, every month, any day-of-week — the first day of every month at 03:00 UTC. "0 3 0 1 * *" would fire at 00:03 — the field order is wrong. A Logic App recurrence adds a second managed service and a single point of failure for what a single trigger handles natively. Event Grid does not emit a calendar-based system event tied to month boundaries.

questions.q: An Azure Function on the Consumption plan must process up to 5,000 messages per second from Service Bus, but you observe scale-out is too slow. Which plan should you switch to for predictable, faster scale and no cold starts?
choices: Premium plan with pre-warmed instance pools
Container Apps with KEDA event-driven scaling
Dedicated (App Service) plan with autoscale rules
Flex Consumption plan in its default no-pre-warm mode
questions.explanation: Functions Premium plan provides pre-warmed instances (no cold start), VNet integration and faster event-driven scale-out than Consumption while still billing per execution. Dedicated (App Service) plan does not scale automatically on event volume — it requires metric-based autoscale rules that lag queue bursts. Container Apps is a separate product, not a Functions hosting plan. Flex Consumption supports always-ready instances but only when explicitly configured — its default behaviour still cold-starts new instances, so it does not satisfy the requirement out of the box.

questions.q: Which Azure Storage service should be used to host static website assets (HTML, CSS, JS) directly served from a custom domain over HTTPS at the lowest cost?
choices: Azure Table Storage with row-key partitioning by URL path
Azure Files SMB share mounted by the web tier for content
Azure Queue Storage configured for browser read-only access
Azure Blob Storage with the Static website feature on $web
questions.explanation: Blob Storage has a Static website feature that exposes the $web container at a primary endpoint, supports custom domains and CDN/Front Door for HTTPS termination — the cheapest way to host SPAs and static sites. Azure Files exposes SMB/NFS shares for application data — it is not an HTTPS web origin. Queue Storage stores messages, not browsable files. Table Storage stores key-value rows and cannot serve arbitrary content over HTTP.

questions.q: A developer must grant a web app running on App Service permission to read secrets from Azure Key Vault WITHOUT storing any credentials in code or config. Which approach is correct?
choices: Service principal whose client secret is set as an App Service Configuration value
Key Vault primary access key referenced from an App Setting at startup
System-assigned managed identity granted Key Vault Get on secrets
Long-lived SAS token cached by the app at first start-up
questions.explanation: Managed identities provide an automatically rotated Microsoft Entra identity to Azure resources. App Service uses this identity to authenticate to Key Vault — no credentials in code or configuration. After enabling the system-assigned identity, grant it Get on secrets via access policies or RBAC. The other options all store a long-lived credential somewhere reachable from source, Configuration or in-memory — an App Setting is just a portal-visible string, a SAS token is still a bearer credential, and a client secret in Configuration is still committed/visible to operators. Key Vault also has no "primary access key" — that is a Storage concept.

correct.useCase: The deployment and management layer for Azure — it handles every request, enforces RBAC, and deploys ARM/Bicep templates.

distractors.useCase: Fails resources over to a secondary region.

nodes.title: Azure messaging services (AZ-204 / AZ-305): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Azure offers three distinct messaging services with very different guarantees: Service Bus for reliable ordered enterprise messaging, Event Grid for event-driven routing, and Event Hubs for high-volume streaming. The AZ-204 exam tests which service fits a given architecture requirement — picking the wrong one is the most common scenario-question trap.

flashcards.front: Service Bus queues vs topics/subscriptions — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Queue: a single sender → single receiver FIFO channel with at-most-once or at-least-once delivery, sessions for ordered processing, and dead-letter queue for undeliverable messages. Topics/subscriptions: a single sender → multiple receivers via subscriber filters — one message fan-out to N subscribers, each with their own queue. Use queues for point-to-point work distribution; use topics when multiple independent consumers need the same message.

flashcards.front: Azure Event Grid — what makes it different from Service Bus?
flashcards.back: Event Grid is a push-based, serverless event routing service — publishers emit events, Event Grid routes them to subscribers based on event type and subject filters. It's optimized for routing discrete events (a blob was created, a VM status changed) to multiple endpoints (Functions, Logic Apps, webhooks) with at-least-once delivery and no persistence beyond ~24 hours. Use Event Grid for reactive, fan-out event notifications; use Service Bus when you need guaranteed ordering, sessions, or long-term message retention.

flashcards.front: Azure Event Hubs — what is its core primitive and what is it used for?
flashcards.back: Event Hubs uses partitions — a stream is divided into N parallel partitions, each an ordered sequence of events. Consumers read from partitions via consumer groups (multiple independent apps each read the full stream through their own group). Retention is configurable (1–90 days). Use Event Hubs for high-throughput streaming: telemetry ingestion, click-stream analytics, log aggregation feeding into Stream Analytics, Spark, or Flink. It is NOT a message queue — ordering is per-partition only, not global.

flashcards.front: Dead-letter queue (DLQ) — what sends a message there?
flashcards.back: A dead-letter queue captures messages that cannot be processed: the message exceeded its max delivery count (retried too many times), its TTL (time-to-live) expired before delivery, or a receiver explicitly dead-lettered it due to a processing error. Both Service Bus queues and topic subscriptions have DLQs. Monitor the DLQ depth in production — messages accumulating there means your processing logic has a bug or the message schema is unexpected.

questions.q: An application needs to receive a notification within seconds when a new blob is uploaded to a container, with built-in filtering on file extension. Which Azure service provides the BEST event delivery?
choices: Event Grid subscription on the storage account with a suffix filter
Function polling the container every 30 seconds with list-blobs
Service Bus topic populated by every uploader with a SQL filter
Storage Queue written by the uploader on each new blob
questions.explanation: Azure Event Grid integrates with Storage and pushes Blob Created events with subject prefix and suffix filters (for example, subject ending in .jpg), giving low-latency server-push notifications. Polling is wasteful, adds latency up to the poll interval, and burns LIST request charges. Service Bus topics are not connected to Storage events out of the box — they only fire if the uploader publishes a message. A Storage Queue written by the uploader couples producers to consumers and breaks when files arrive via tools that bypass the uploader (AzCopy, Storage Explorer, REST).

questions.q: A B2B integration needs a managed Azure messaging service that delivers messages FIFO within a logical conversation and rejects repeat MessageIds inside a configurable sliding window — both server-side, without bespoke application logic. Which service supports both natively?
choices: Azure Storage Queues with poison-message handling and visibility timeouts
Azure Event Grid with subject filters and at-least-once delivery semantics
Azure Service Bus queues with sessions and duplicate detection enabled
Azure Event Hubs with partition keys and consumer-group checkpointing
questions.explanation: Service Bus queues support sessions (ordered FIFO delivery per session ID) and duplicate detection (rejects messages with the same MessageId within a configurable 20-second to 7-day window). Event Hubs preserves order within a partition but has no built-in MessageId deduplication — it is a streaming log, not a deduping broker. Event Grid is push-style event distribution with at-least-once delivery and no FIFO or dedup guarantees. Storage Queues offer only best-effort FIFO and no native deduplication.

questions.q: A web API protects endpoints with Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD). A daemon service running on a VM must call the API without any user interaction. Which OAuth 2.0 flow is appropriate?
choices: Implicit flow returning tokens directly in the URL fragment
Client Credentials flow authenticated with a certificate
Authorization Code flow with PKCE for public clients
Device Code flow polling the token endpoint for approval
questions.explanation: Client Credentials flow is designed for service-to-service and daemon scenarios with no user — the client authenticates with its own credentials (client ID + certificate or secret) to obtain an access token. Authorization Code with PKCE is for interactive end users in single-page or native apps. Implicit flow is deprecated and was always intended for browser-based clients, never for a confidential daemon. Device Code is for input-constrained user devices like TVs and CLIs, where a user types a code on another device — there is no user here to approve.

questions.q: Which Microsoft Graph permission type should a multi-tenant SaaS app request to read user mail on behalf of the signed-in user?
choices: Application permission Directory.AccessAsUser.All with admin consent
Application permission Mail.Read with tenant-wide admin consent
App-only permission Mail.ReadWrite.All scoped to the app
Delegated permission Mail.Read with user consent
questions.explanation: Delegated permissions act on behalf of the signed-in user and are scoped to that user's mailbox. Mail.Read (delegated) is the least-privileged scope that satisfies the requirement. Application permissions are app-only (no user) and access every mailbox in the tenant — over-broad here and requiring tenant-admin consent. Directory.AccessAsUser.All targets the directory, not mail (and despite its name it is still an application permission). Mail.ReadWrite.All adds write permission that is not needed and is also app-only.

questions.q: A developer wants to deliver a dynamic web app globally with low latency, automatic HTTPS, custom domains and a managed CDN — without provisioning a CDN profile manually. Which option is BEST?
choices: Application Gateway v2 fronting one region with autoscale enabled
Traffic Manager profile using priority routing across regions
Azure CDN Standard from Microsoft tier with custom origin
Azure Front Door Standard or Premium profile
questions.explanation: Azure Front Door is a global Layer-7 load balancer with built-in CDN caching, WAF, automatic HTTPS via managed certificates and split-TCP for low TTFB on dynamic content — no separate CDN profile required. Azure CDN profiles cache static content but do not load-balance dynamic origins across regions on their own and still require a profile. Traffic Manager is DNS-based steering only — it does not terminate TLS or cache. Application Gateway is regional, so it cannot deliver low latency globally without per-region deployment and external traffic steering.

questions.q: Which Azure App Configuration feature lets a developer roll out a new feature to 10% of users and progressively increase the rollout WITHOUT redeploying the app?
choices: Configuration snapshots pinned to a named release tag
Feature flags with a Targeting filter
Key-value pairs scoped by labels per environment
Managed identity bound to the App Service plan
questions.explanation: App Configuration feature flags support filters: Targeting (percentage rollout, user/group lists), Time Window and Custom. The Targeting filter lets you specify a default rollout percentage and per-group overrides without code changes — the client reads the new value at refresh time. Labels organize config across environments but do not toggle features. Snapshots are immutable point-in-time copies for rollback, not progressive delivery. Managed identities solve authentication between App Service and App Configuration, not feature exposure.

questions.q: An ARM template deployment must reference a secret stored in Key Vault at deployment time without exposing the value in deployment logs. Which technique is correct?
choices: Use the @description() decorator on a secure parameter pointing at the Key Vault
Hard-code the secret in the parameters file and gitignore the file
Reference the secret in the parameters file via keyVault and secretName
Pass the secret on the az deployment group create command line
questions.explanation: ARM and Bicep deployments dereference Key Vault secrets directly in the parameters file using a reference object: { "reference": { "keyVault": { "id": "..." }, "secretName": "..." } }. Azure Resource Manager fetches the secret at deploy time and never writes the value to deployment logs. @description() documents a Bicep parameter and never resolves a secret; making the parameter @secure() suppresses log output but does not retrieve a Key Vault value on its own. Hard-coding the value puts plaintext in source history; passing it on the CLI puts it in shell history and process listings.

nodes.title: Process uploads serverlessly

data.scenario: Users upload files to storage; process each one and save the result. No servers to manage.

nodes.explanation: A blob upload raises an Event Grid event, which triggers an Azure Function that processes the file and writes the results to Cosmos DB — event-driven, no servers.

nodes.title: Observability and monitoring: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Observability is metrics + logs + traces — the three pillars. You need all three to debug a production incident: metrics tell you something is wrong, logs tell you what happened, traces tell you where in the call graph the problem lives.

flashcards.front: Metrics vs logs vs traces — what does each tell you?
flashcards.back: Metrics: numeric time-series, cheap to store, perfect for dashboards and alerts ('p99 latency = 800 ms'). Logs: discrete events with context, expensive at scale, perfect for forensics. Traces: causally-linked spans showing a request's full path through services.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between an alert and a notification?
flashcards.back: An alert is a condition that fires when a metric crosses a threshold (CPU > 80% for 5 min). The notification is the resulting message (email, Slack, PagerDuty page). One alert can fan out to many notifications. Tuning alerts is harder than wiring notifications.

flashcards.front: What is an SLI / SLO / SLA?
flashcards.back: SLI (indicator): the metric you actually measure ('% of requests under 200 ms'). SLO (objective): the internal target ('99.9% of requests under 200 ms over 28 days'). SLA (agreement): the contractual promise to customers, usually weaker than the SLO so you have buffer.

Plain-text logs are unparseable at scale. Structured logs (JSON, with timestamp + level + service + request_id + key fields) are indexable, queryable, and join-able across services. Most platforms auto-extract fields from JSON without configuration.

questions.q: An APIM product applies a generous shared rate limit. The team wants to additionally cap one specific subscription's calls per minute, without changing limits for other subscribers on the same product. Which inbound policy should be added?
choices: quota-by-key scoped to the subscription on a daily renewal period
rate-limit-by-key scoped to the subscription key for a 60-second window
set-backend-service rewriting the upstream URL for that subscription
ip-filter restricting the subscription to a specific source IP range
questions.explanation: rate-limit-by-key applies a per-key throttle (typically per subscription key) on top of any product-wide limit and resets on a configurable short window — exactly matching a per-minute cap on one subscription. quota-by-key enforces longer-period volume caps (per hour, day, week, month) and resets only on the renewal-period boundary — wrong granularity. set-backend-service rewrites the upstream URL and does not throttle. ip-filter restricts source IPs and does not implement rate limiting.

questions.q: A developer wants to monitor an Azure Function with distributed tracing, exception capture and live metrics. Which service should they integrate?
choices: Azure Monitor Logs only, with custom Kusto alert rules
Azure Service Health combined with resource health probes
Network Watcher packet capture on the function host plan
Application Insights with auto-instrumentation enabled
questions.explanation: Application Insights is the APM service for Azure apps — it captures requests, dependencies, exceptions and traces across services with correlation IDs (distributed tracing) and offers Live Metrics and Smart Detection. Azure Monitor Logs is the underlying log store; on its own it lacks APM correlation and live metrics. Service Health reports Azure platform incidents that affect a subscription, not application-level telemetry. Network Watcher inspects packets and routes, not function-level traces or exceptions.

questions.q: An engineer opens the Application Insights Logs blade and writes ad-hoc queries that use `where`, `project`, `summarize`, and time-series operators. Which query language does that blade execute?
choices: Kusto Query Language, shared across Log Analytics and Microsoft Sentinel
Transact-SQL, the language used in Azure SQL Database and Synapse
Lucene query syntax, originally popularised by Elasticsearch and Solr
GraphQL queries with field selection and nested resolver execution paths
questions.explanation: Application Insights and Azure Monitor Logs use Kusto Query Language (KQL) — the same dialect as Azure Data Explorer and Microsoft Sentinel. Example: requests | where timestamp > ago(1h) | summarize count() by resultCode. T-SQL has a where clause but uses SELECT/GROUP BY rather than project/summarize, and runs in Azure SQL Database and Synapse, not Monitor. Lucene powers full-text search engines like Elasticsearch and Azure Cognitive Search, but is not the Monitor query language. GraphQL is an API query language for application servers, not a Monitor log dialect.

questions.q: Which Azure Container Apps feature is BEST suited to scale a service to zero when idle and back up on incoming HTTP traffic?
choices: Azure VM Scale Set integration provisioned via Bicep
Dapr sidecar with pub/sub and state-store bindings
KEDA-based scale rule using the HTTP scaler
Manual scale rule pinned to a fixed replica count
questions.explanation: Azure Container Apps uses KEDA under the hood. The HTTP scaler scales 0→N based on concurrent request volume per replica, including scale-to-zero when traffic stops. Dapr provides service-to-service primitives like pub/sub and state — it is orthogonal to scaling. Manual replica counts cannot reach zero on idle. VM Scale Sets are a different compute product entirely and are not used to scale Container Apps replicas.

questions.q: A developer needs to generate a time-limited URL that grants read-only access to a single blob without sharing the storage account key. Which feature should they use?
choices: Anonymous public container access on the blob endpoint
User delegation SAS or service SAS scoped to the blob
Stored access policy attached to a queue at account scope
Account-level shared access signature for the storage account
questions.explanation: A service SAS — or, preferably, a user delegation SAS signed by Entra ID credentials — targets a specific blob with read-only permission and an expiry. The user delegation form does not require the account key at all. An account-level SAS grants access across services and is broader than needed. Anonymous public access removes authentication entirely and grants the same access to everyone. A stored access policy on a queue applies to queues, not blobs, and only revokes existing SAS tokens — it does not by itself generate a URL.

questions.q: Which Azure Cognitive Search feature lets a developer surface results enriched with AI-generated metadata (e.g., key phrases, OCR text) extracted from PDFs and images?
choices: Skillsets and indexers running cognitive enrichment
Synonym maps that alias query terms at search time
Suggesters that power as-you-type autocomplete entries
Scoring profiles that re-rank results by field weighting
questions.explanation: Skillsets attach AI skills (OCR, key phrase extraction, entity recognition, custom Web API skills) to an indexer pipeline, projecting enriched fields into the search index. Suggesters drive autocomplete from existing index fields but cannot extract new metadata. Scoring profiles tune relevance weighting at query time without adding new fields. Synonym maps rewrite query terms with alternate forms — they neither read documents nor produce new content.
